title: Trump Says Iran Talks to Resume Monday After Calling Off Planned Strikes
excerpt: The US president declined to set a deadline for a deal as oil prices fell sharply, while Iran's foreign minister held calls with Saudi and Pakistani counterparts on diplomatic efforts.
body:
• Trump said negotiations with Iran would begin Monday afternoon after calling off an imminent military strike over the weekend.
  • The US suspended a two-week bombing campaign against Iran on Saturday, and oil prices fell more than 4 percent in early Monday trading.
  • Iran's foreign minister held calls with Saudi and Pakistani counterparts, while Tehran denied requesting negotiations, calling such reports "fabricated."
  • The Strait of Hormuz, a conduit for 20 percent of global oil and LNG shipments, remains largely under Iranian control.

From Threats to Talks — Again

President Donald Trump said Sunday that negotiations with Iran would take place Monday afternoon, declining to set a deadline for a deal after abruptly calling off a planned military strike in hopes of reaching an agreement to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and resolve the standoff over Tehran's nuclear capabilities.

https://x.com/CNBC/status/2084103909010739703

Trump had announced late Saturday on Truth Social that Iran and other Middle Eastern countries had requested time to finalise a deal that would lead to "the Immediate, Complete and Total" reopening of the strait and "an end to Iran's nuclear threat," according to Reuters. He warned that Tehran must "rapidly make a DEAL."

"Would I rather make a deal? I'm not looking to kill people because people die, a lot of people die, and we don't want that."

— Donald Trump, US President

A Five-Month War With No Resolution

The latest de-escalation marks another twist in the US-Iran conflict, which began when Trump launched military operations alongside Israel in late February. Over five months, the war has expanded from targeted strikes to a broader regional conflagration involving Gulf states, the Red Sea, and even a Mediterranean facility in Egypt.

The US had carried out air strikes on Iran for 13 consecutive nights before abruptly suspending the campaign on Friday. The bombing killed scores of people and destroyed bridges, tunnels, and military targets across southern Iran. Four US service members were killed by Iranian return fire against American bases in neighbouring Arab states.

US military commanders had advised Trump they were running out of targets, according to a US official who spoke to Reuters. The chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, General Dan Caine, raised concerns about the depletion of air munitions. Trump dismissed suggestions of shortages, saying the military was "rapidly rebuilding inventories."

Tehran's Diplomatic Moves

Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi held phone calls with Saudi counterpart Prince Faisal bin Farhan and Pakistan's army chief Asim Munir to discuss diplomatic efforts, Iranian state media reported Sunday.

Tehran's official news agency IRNA reported that negotiations between Iran and Oman over the Strait of Hormuz were in their "final stages." But Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei pushed back on the framing, saying the talks concerned a new shipping route through the strait and had "no link to the Strait of Hormuz being opened or closed."

Iran has largely closed the strait — a conduit for 20 percent of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas before the war — causing energy prices to surge and stoking inflation globally. Last month, Tehran publicly rejected an Omani proposal, backed by Gulf states, to jointly manage the waterway.

Oil Markets React

The prospect of renewed diplomacy sent oil prices tumbling. Brent crude, which briefly topped $100 a barrel last week, fell more than 4 percent in early Monday trading. The commodity had dropped as low as $87.55 during the previous week's trading before stabilising near $89.

Trump has argued that keeping Iran from acquiring nuclear weapons justifies higher fuel costs in the near term, but the economic pain has put increasing political pressure on his administration to find a resolution.

Israel Keeps Options Open

Israel's Energy Minister Eli Cohen, a member of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's security cabinet, said there was close intelligence coordination between Israel and the US but warned that Israel would act independently if needed.

"With or without an agreement, and regardless of any external commitments, if Iran attempts to renew its nuclear program or advance its ballistic missile industries, we will be there," Cohen said.

A June framework agreement had set an end-of-August deadline for comprehensive talks, but the two sides have disputed the memorandum's language on the strait — with Washington insisting it requires free passage and Tehran maintaining it authorises supervised transit. Monday's talks could determine whether that framework survives.
